Essays/The-Cost-of-Needing-to-Understand.title: The Cost of Needing to Understand Everything
Essays/The-Cost-of-Needing-to-Understand.content:
On bottom-up thinking, the bad memory that isn’t, and learning to trust the box

Some people can open a textbook the night before an exam, skim it, and walk out with good marks. If you’ve always envied them and never managed it yourself, see whether any of this sounds familiar:

You can’t learn a fact until you know why it’s true. Being told isn’t enough; you need to see it derived.
Subjects you can rebuild from a few principles come easily. Subjects that arrive as a pile of facts and exceptions feel impossible.
You’ve read the whole theory of something and never actually used it.
Your notes never get going, because you don’t understand the topic well enough to write them yet.
You look at an architecture diagram, a page of boxes and arrows, and nothing sticks.
Somewhere along the way, you decided you just have a bad memory.

I was like this for most of my life. I want to describe how it works, what it costs, and the odd moment it flipped, because I don’t think the problem is memory at all.
A good observation turned into a law
Somewhere around class eight, I made myself a rule. If I studied something, I’d understand it to the core. Otherwise it was a waste of time: I’d read it, forget it, and be left with nothing.
There was something true in that. Deep understanding is the kind that lasts, and the kind you can build on. The mistake was turning a useful observation into a law. Once it was a law, my mind simply refused to work with information it didn’t fully understand.
Call this bottom-up thinking. You start at the foundations and build upward, and you won’t stand on any floor until you’ve personally checked every floor below it. Top-down thinking goes the other way. You start with the big picture, accept its parts as given, and dig into the details only where you need to.
What bottom-up costs
The main cost is the price of entry. Before I could reason about even basic things in a subject, I had to build a deep, concrete model of how it worked.
In school this sorted subjects for me in a way I didn’t understand at the time. Geometry was easy because I could see it; algebra took much longer. Vectors were fine because I could picture arrows moving. Matrices and determinants were a grey zone, because I couldn’t picture what a determinant was. Chemistry was a disaster. It’s full of rules with exceptions, facts you’re expected to hold without deriving them, and I couldn’t hold them. I concluded that my memory was bad.
The same pattern followed me out of school. For years I wanted to get into machine learning. I read Michael Nielsen’s Neural Networks and Deep Learning and understood it down to the mathematics of how a network learns. I never trained a single model. For someone who thought the way I did, working in machine learning would have meant doing a PhD first, because I couldn’t act on anything I didn’t fully understand.
That’s the real shape of it. It isn’t laziness, and it isn’t a bad memory. It’s an inability to act under uncertainty.
The workarounds
Software made the problem impossible to ignore. Nobody can understand a modern software stack to the bottom; there’s far too much of it. The whole field runs on abstraction. You use things whose source you’ve never read, and you trust that they do what they say.
My mind wouldn’t do that, so I found a way around it. When I met a system I didn’t have time to learn properly, I’d invent a hypothetical version of it out of building blocks I already understood: things I’d seen working in real code, mechanisms I could picture end to end. How might the internet move a page from a server to my screen? How might a regex engine actually match a pattern? How might Git store history? For Kubernetes, I’d imagine how I would build it myself from parts I’d used before. The guesses didn’t have to be right. They only had to be made of real things, so that my mind would accept them.
This can sound like abstraction, but it’s the opposite. An abstraction asks you to accept a component by what it does, without knowing what it’s made of. My hypothetical models did the reverse. I couldn’t accept anything my mind couldn’t trace down to concrete parts, so when I didn’t have the real mechanism, I made up one that was plausible. It was still bottom-up thinking, just with invented foundations instead of real ones.
It worked, more or less, and it gave me a solid base for my job. Depth wasn’t useless either: in the few areas I understood well, it sometimes let me see an unusual way through. But every new system still needed its own homemade model before I could reason about it, and every one of them cost a lot to build. I was never going to be the person who learns it the night before.
The flip
The change came from somewhere unexpected: I was trying to work out how to organise my notes.
Note-taking had always been hard for me, and now I can see why. You take notes before you understand a subject, while it’s still half-formed. I couldn’t. My instinct was that my notes had to mirror reality. They were meant to document how things actually are, in my own words, so I could look at them later and recall the mechanics. You can’t mirror something you don’t understand yet, so I was stuck.
Then I thought about a biology textbook. If it mirrored reality, it would need a separate chapter for every human being, because that’s how we exist: billions of separate bodies with a lot in common. A textbook doesn’t do that. It describes one model body, organised into parts, and inside each part it describes the variants. The chapter on blood covers group A and group B, though no one has both. The book isn’t a copy of anyone. It’s a structure of its own, built so you can make sense of any real body you meet.
That was the realisation. Notes don’t mirror reality. They exist in their own right. An abstraction, a model, a box on a diagram is as real as anything made of atoms. It’s real in a different way, because its job is to help you move through reality rather than copy it. (It’s the same idea as in Logic Isn’t About Truth: a model has to be useful, not a replica.)
This probably comes naturally to a lot of people. For me it was a gift.
What changed
The first thing that changed was the architecture diagrams. I’d never really been able to look at Kubernetes, and the problem was never the diagram. It was that I didn’t respect the boxes. I didn’t believe in a component until I’d rebuilt it in my head from real parts. Once I accepted that the box is the thing, at least at that level, the diagrams started to stick.
Which suggests the “bad memory” was never about memory. There’s a well-known study from 1973. The psychologists William Chase and Herbert Simon showed chess positions to masters and beginners for a few seconds, then asked them to rebuild the board from memory. The masters did far better, but only on positions from real games. When the pieces were placed at random, the masters’ advantage mostly disappeared. They didn’t have better memories. They saw the board as chunks, meaningful patterns they already knew, and they remembered the chunks. Memory needs something to hang on. If your mind won’t accept the hooks, nothing sticks.
Other things followed:

I could take notes on half the picture, knowing I’d revise them.
I could start using something before I fully understood it, and let the use teach me.
I could act on less information, which is most of what people mean by high agency. Games like chess and poker may reward the same habit: you reason with patterns and odds, never with the whole picture.
I could work in a team. As a bottom-up thinker I couldn’t have worked with ten people, because nobody can understand everyone’s work to the bottom. You reason with the components other people built, and you trust their edges.

Now I build abstract components, treat them as real, and reason with them entirely inside the model. I no longer force each one back down to something physical first.
Why some subjects felt illogical
Looking back, chemistry wasn’t illogical, and neither are biology, finance or most of the things I avoided. These subjects work with partial information and real uncertainty. Chemistry has exceptions because the underlying physics is far too complicated to work out from scratch every time, so it gets summarised in rules that mostly hold. Financial models never fully describe a market. The people in these fields aren’t being sloppy. They’re doing the only thing anyone can when there’s more information than one person can hold: build high-level models, use them, and amend them as they learn.
If you’re a bottom-up thinker, the way in looks something like this:

Start from the top. Learn the main parts and how they connect before learning any one part in depth.
Treat the boxes as real. A component you don’t understand inside is still something you can reason with.
Go deeper only where the top fails. If the high-level model explains what you see, leave it. Dig into the one place where it doesn’t.
Expect to revise. A first model is meant to be replaced. It isn’t a promise.

That’s all it took: a change in what I counted as real. It came while I was organising my notes.

Essays/The-Scarcity-That-Survives.title: The Scarcity That Survives
Essays/The-Scarcity-That-Survives.content:
Why abundance solves production, not wanting


                  
                  Draft 
                  
                

This essay is still being revised.



We have always overestimated how much a new thing will change our lives. That goes for one person with a raise or a new house, and for a society with electric light or the internet. We picture the difference it will make, and then we adapt to it. This essay looks at AGI the same way, through hedonic adaptation.
In 1930, in the depths of the Great Depression, John Maynard Keynes sat down to predict the world his grandchildren would inherit. Within a hundred years, he argued, productivity growth would all but solve the economic problem. His grandchildren would work fifteen-hour weeks, and their hard problem would not be scarcity but its opposite:

“For the first time since his creation man will be faced with his real, his permanent problem — how to use his freedom from pressing economic cares, how to occupy the leisure, which science and compound interest will have won for him, to live wisely and agreeably and well.”

He got the first half exactly right. Output per person in the rich world has outrun even his guess. The second half never came. Nobody works fifteen hours. We took the productivity and spent it on more — more work, more wants, whole new races that didn’t exist when he wrote.
The easy way to tell this story is that Keynes misunderstood people. He didn’t. In the same essay he split human needs in two: needs that are “absolute in the sense that we feel them whatever the situation of our fellow human beings may be,” and needs that are “relative in the sense that we feel them only if their satisfaction lifts us above, makes us feel superior to, our fellows.” The relative needs, he wrote, “may indeed be insatiable; for the higher the general level, the higher still are they.” He saw the treadmill too: the purposive man who is always after “jam to-morrow and never jam to-day.” Nearly everything this essay argues, Keynes saw in 1930.
He bet on hope anyway, and the bet was narrow. He wagered that once the absolute needs were met, we would walk away from the relative race and turn to “the art of life itself.” We didn’t. We poured the surplus straight back into the race.
A century later, the utopian case for AGI-era universal basic income makes the same bet without his caution: production becomes effectively infinite, so work becomes optional, so we are finally free to consume and rest. Underneath it is a picture of desire as a checklist — a finite set of things we want and can’t yet afford — where the wanting stops once production ticks off the last item. Keynes knew the relative needs had no last item and hoped we’d stop chasing them. This essay is about why we won’t, and why AGI can’t make us.
Let me put the conclusion up front. With respect to the thing we actually chase — call it contentment, the sense of having arrived — AGI, the most hyped technology in history, is going to be a non-event. Not because it changes little; it changes almost everything outside the skull. But the set point inside the skull doesn’t move. This is the argument for why.
The treadmill
Everyone has felt this from the inside. You get the thing you wanted, and almost at once something better swims into view — sometimes not even better across the board, just a different trade whose downside looks survivable from a distance. Psychologists named the machinery: the hedonic treadmill. The famous demonstration compared people who had just won large lottery jackpots against people who had just been paralyzed in accidents. Within a year both groups had drifted back toward where they started, and the winners reported taking measurably less pleasure in ordinary daily life. You reach the thing, and the set point quietly resets beneath you.
Look at what “better” even means as it slides around, and the options sort along a single axis — ranked by how completely production can flood each. Nearest is utility: it works faster, lasts longer, the axis everyone assumes desire runs on. Then quantity: more of the same. Then novelty: it’s new, which is enough. Then aesthetics: it’s more beautiful. And at the far end, the one that never bottoms out — story: what the thing says about you, who it places you above. A machine given a century will drown utility, quantity, novelty, most of aesthetics. It never touches the last one.
Which tells you what desire is made of. The wanting comes first; the reason comes second. We live it the other way round — I want this one because it’s faster, because it’s rarer — but the reason is manufactured after the fact to fit a wanting already running. This isn’t borrowed metaphor; it’s how the machine is built. People have almost no direct access to why they choose what they choose: asked, they don’t introspect, they invent a plausible story and report it as fact. When the mute half of a surgically split brain is shown an instruction and acts on it, the speaking half instantly fabricates a confident reason for a decision it never saw. Swap the item someone picked a moment ago and hand it back as their choice, and most won’t notice — they’ll argue fluently for a preference they never had.
So be exact about what’s fake, because everything downstream depends on it. The drive is real. The restlessness is real, and it is prior to every object it fastens onto. What gets invented is the story about which object will finally quiet it — and that story is wrong every time, because the object was never the point. The restlessness is the constant. The thing is interchangeable.
There’s a famous version of this idea, and it’s half right — the missing half is the one that matters. René Girard argued that beyond raw appetite we don’t know what to want, so we borrow our wants from other people: desire is imitation, and two people reaching for the same thing is the seed of every rivalry in history. He put copying at the root. But copying isn’t a root — it’s a strategy. The substrate ships with a short list of primary drives, and one of them is as old and as serious as hunger: the drive for rank. It isn’t learned. It shows up in infants before they can speak, who already expect the bigger, higher figure to prevail; it runs in every primate troop; and after decades of looking, the desire for standing turns out to be universal, present across every culture anyone has measured. We don’t copy other people’s desires because copying is what desire is. We copy them because wanting what a higher-ranked person has is itself a move in the status game — and of all the primary drives, rank is the one that never reports back satisfied. Girard saw the imitation and mistook it for the cause. What he was looking at was a species that keeps score.
And keeping score is the one axis still standing after the machine has flooded all the others.
There’s an obvious objection: the monk, the contemplative, the person who deliberately wants less. They’re real, and they prove the rule rather than breaking it. Every tradition that quiets the craving does it the same way — not by acquiring the last item on the list but by years of deliberate practice aimed at switching off the wanting itself, a lifetime of effort running against the grain of the machinery. That the exit exists, and that it costs that much to reach, tells you exactly how hard the default is wired in.
From utility to status
Watch any product category grow old. It arrives competing on what it does: a faster processor, a battery that lasts the day, a pigment that holds its color. While utility is scarce it maps straight onto lived experience — the thing does your labor, spares your body, hands back your time. But utility is the one dimension technology exists to demolish. Solve it and it can no longer tell anyone apart from anyone: once the fast processor sits in every pocket, no one earns a sliver of standing by owning one. The wanting doesn’t die. It migrates to whatever is still scarce — and what stays scarce is whatever is hardest to hand to everyone at once.
For most of recorded history, purple wasn’t a color you chose. It was a rank. Tyrian purple came from the crushed glands of sea snails — thousands of them for a gram of dye, barely enough to edge a single robe — and Rome eventually wrote the exclusivity into law: the deepest purple was the emperor’s alone, and to be caught wearing it uninvited could cost you your head. “To wear the purple” simply meant to take the throne. The dye never sold a color. It sold the fact that almost no one else was allowed to have it.
Aluminum tells the same story in reverse, and we got to watch the collapse in real time. In the 1850s it outpriced gold; when the Washington Monument was capped in 1884, the cap was a small aluminum pyramid, shown off in Tiffany’s window before it was hauled to the top. Napoleon III is said to have served his most honored guests on aluminum and left everyone else with gold. Then a new smelting process arrived, the price fell through the floor, and aluminum became the foil we wrap a sandwich in and throw away. Nothing about the metal changed. What changed is that everyone could have it — and the moment everyone could, no one wanted it.
The wristwatch is the mechanism caught in the act. In the 1970s, quartz movements made mechanical watches obsolete on every utilitarian axis — a 30 quartz keeps better time than a 300,000 Patek Philippe. The Swiss industry nearly died, then discovered that the inferiority was the product. Mechanical watches are worth more now than ever, precisely because they are handmade, inefficient, and scarce. Utility didn’t just leave the category; its absence became the pitch.
Or run it forward. Take a smartphone five hundred years into the past and it becomes the most coveted object on Earth, something kings would go to war over. Today it’s nothing, because everyone has one. If everyone has a thing, it isn’t really a thing anyone wants; it becomes the baseline, and desire re-anchors just above it.
It’s tempting to read this as a ladder — function, then aesthetics, then meaning, then story, each rung finer than the last. It isn’t a ladder, and nothing makes the rungs arrive in that order. Aesthetics and novelty and story don’t wait their turn; they compete in parallel the instant utility stops being decisive. What actually sorts them is a single property: how much of a thing’s value depends on someone else not having it. Utility barely depends on that — a fast chip works just as well whether or not your neighbor owns one. Status depends on nothing else — it is the gap. So as production saturates the dimensions that need no loser, desire gets squeezed onto the ones that do, until all that’s left at the bottom of the funnel is the dimension made entirely of other people: rank. (Economists named the tail of this a century ago — conspicuous consumption, goods whose whole function is to be seen being owned.)
Why technology can’t touch it
Here is the structural reason, and it’s the heart of the argument. Divide the world’s goods in two. Material goods — food, energy, housing, compute — can in principle be made in greater quantity for everyone at once. Positional goods — status, exclusivity, being first, being best, the address everyone recognizes — are defined by their scarcity. They can’t be mass-produced even in principle, because their value is the ranking. If everyone stands on tiptoe to see better, no one sees better; the effort cancels and only the strain remains.
AGI is a machine for growing the material side, maybe without limit. It has no purchase on the positional side, and the reason is arithmetic: rank is zero-sum. For someone to be above average, someone else has to be below it; there will only ever be one most-admired person in any given room. You can manufacture infinite goods, but you cannot manufacture a world where everyone is above the median, because the median rises to meet them.
You’d expect technology to at least widen the arena, and for broadcast fame it did — mass media and the internet built ranking systems with follower counts in the billions. But the status that actually presses on a life is the reciprocal kind, standing among the people whose regard you can feel, and that circle is capped by the same cognition it always was. The ceiling has a name: Dunbar’s number, the roughly 150 stable relationships a person can carry, read straight off brain anatomy — across primate species the size of the social group tracks the size of the neocortex, and the human brain plugs into that curve at about 150. A billion followers never raised it, because the bottleneck was never the tooling. It was the cortex doing the bookkeeping — the same cortex reading this sentence.
One caveat fences the whole essay. I’m assuming the substrate holds still. If AGI ends up reaching in and rewriting the human hardware itself — editing the machinery that manufactures wanting and rank-hunger and restlessness — then every prediction here is void, and honestly the question gets too fuzzy to reason about. So I’m not asking it. The question I am asking is narrower and answerable: what does it feel like to be a human — this human, the one doing the predicting — in a world where everything outside us has changed and we haven’t?
Solving material scarcity, then, doesn’t end the race. It relocates the entire race into the positional economy — the one place production can’t reach. The social axis of desire is the scarcity that survives. Not because people are shallow, but because it’s the only axis on which scarcity is mathematically conserved.
A world with only social scarcity
From here on, the specifics are guesses. The mechanism underneath them isn’t.
From any single person’s vantage, the world after material scarcity looks strangely familiar: the same rat race, different tokens. And this isn’t a new observation dressed up as a prediction — it’s the oldest pattern we have. Sorting into ranks is a human universal in the strict anthropological sense: of the traits catalogued as appearing in every society ever documented, prestige, status distinction, and the dance of dominance and deference are all on the list. There is no record of a human group that didn’t sort itself.
The tempting objection is the hunter-gatherer band — flat, sharing, no chiefs. Look closer and the band becomes the best evidence, not the counterexample. Foragers stay flat only through relentless work: they mock the boaster, shame the hoarder, ignore the man who tries to give orders, drive out the one who won’t stop. Anthropologists call it a reverse dominance hierarchy — a coalition of everyone, permanently pushing down on anyone who tries to rise. Egalitarianism isn’t the absence of the status drive; it’s a society spending its entire moral energy to suppress a drive that never switches off. The good hunter still has to bring the meat home — he just has to belittle his own kill while he hands it over. The tokens change; the game underneath is identical.
Which means we don’t have to speculate about what happens when you hand people an income floor and make work optional. We’ve been running that experiment for decades. The unhappiness of the long-term unemployed turns out to be mostly not about money: the non-pecuniary cost — the lost structure, purpose, and standing — dwarfs the lost income, and it barely moves when you replace the income. More generous benefits improve the material situation and leave the misery largely intact. Worse, the wound scars — track tens of thousands of people over fifteen years, and unemployment is one of the rare blows a person never fully adapts back from, the set point staying depressed even after they find work again.
Sit with that for a world of universal basic income. The stereotype of the man in his thirties in his parents’ basement is not a story about deprivation — the fridge is full. His suffering is positional: he’s at the bottom of a hierarchy with no visible way up, and no amount of food fixes what was never about food. The post-AGI citizen on a universal stipend is that same figure scaled to a civilization. The work will be nominally optional and not optional at all, because the need to matter among your peers is as real as the hunger in your stomach — and unlike hunger, no machine can fill it.
This is the place to be blunt about what the argument rests on. We treat physical pain — hunger, cold, injury — as real, and mental pain — being outranked, ignored, unneeded — as somehow lesser, a luxury ache for people whose real problems are already solved. That gap is mostly an illusion, and you can measure how small it is. Put someone through an unwanted breakup, show them a photograph of the person who left, slide them into a scanner: what lights up isn’t a dedicated sadness center, it’s the same machinery that fires when a hot probe is pressed to the forearm. Push further — give people ordinary acetaminophen every day for three weeks and they report fewer hurt feelings than people on a placebo. A drug for physical pain dulls social pain. (Not identical down to the neuron — the strict single-region version of that claim has rightly been contested. What survives is sturdier: the two pains share hardware, answer to the same drugs, and drive the same behavior.) So when the argument says positional scarcity produces suffering, it isn’t reaching for a metaphor.
The abstraction bites hardest exactly where you’d least expect it — in money, the most material thing there is. The Easterlin paradox: at any given moment the richer people in a country report more happiness than the poorer ones, yet as an entire country grows richer over decades its average happiness doesn’t budge. Both are true at once only if what registers isn’t how much you have but how much you have relative to the people around you. When everyone rises together, no one rises in the ranking. The cleanest proof came later: hold your own income fixed, and your neighbors earning more makes you report being less happy. Not their poverty dragging you down — their prosperity.
Some of this world we can already sketch. Not by utility — machines win on utility — but by the plain fact of being human, we keep granting each other a premium. You can measure it: show people a wall of paintings, all of them machine-made, and label some “human-created” and some “AI-created” at random. The human-labeled ones get rated more beautiful and more likable — identical pixels, worth more for the story attached. What drove the effect was exactly what a machine can’t supply: the sense of a person behind the work who meant it.
We’ve run the same experiment with our own legs. The car has beaten the fastest human for over a century, and the effect on running was not obsolescence but the opposite — more people ran marathons in 2024 than in any year in history. Nobody stages a marathon to find out whether a car is faster; everyone already knows, and it was never the question, because we never ran to cross the city. Play has always worked this way — irrational by the utilitarian yardstick, which is exactly why it’s universal: children play, young animals play, none of them optimizing anything. Chess makes the point a second time — more played today than at any moment before a computer could crush the world champion, while the strongest engines now play one another in tournaments almost no one watches. Strength was never the draw. The human was.
Follow that premium to the places it doesn’t want to go, because the argument obliges it. If, in a world where machines do everything better, having humans do things for you becomes the luxury, then human attention becomes a scarce good — and scarce goods get owned. So ask it plainly. If status lives on exclusion, and AGI drops the cost of access to zero, does someone re-introduce the exclusion on purpose — gating access to the best intelligence not because gating is necessary but precisely because a thing everyone has is worthless as a marker, and a thing withheld is valuable in exact proportion to the withholding? The technology erases the scarcity; the positional economy has every incentive to legislate it back. And the darker question: if human presence is the last scarce good, does a class of people emerge whose function is simply to be status objects for others — not to produce, since production is free, but to exist as someone else’s audience, ornament, or possession? Positional economies have commodified human beings every time the incentives lined up, and here they line up hard. I’ll leave the question where it is.
Consider the most intimate case. A gift between partners distills the whole logic down to two people: an ornament, beautiful and expensive and completely useless, whose entire value is the message I spent something scarce on you. AGI makes the object free to produce, and this does no more to kill the gift than quartz did to the mechanical watch. It just moves the signal to what stays scarce — that this particular human, out of all the finite hours in a life, chose to point their attention at you. So the dating and courtship economy doesn’t merely survive the arrival of perfect artificial companions; it’s a natural growth sector, because it trades directly in the one commodity that can’t be manufactured. There may be AI partners more attentive and available than any person, and human courtship will go on anyway, probably larger than before — for the same reason people still want a human to have cooked the meal. The point was never the service. It was that a human chose to give it.
Is this utopia? Clearly not — the suffering of rank is fully intact. Is it dystopia? Probably not that either. That’s how boring we are: we adapt, we forget, we re-anchor, and the new world feels normal inside a generation.
Navigating the transition
AGI isn’t arriving on a date; it’s a spectrum, and we’re somewhere along it. For anyone deciding what to get good at: the machines aren’t eating work at random. They eat in a direction.
The direction is this: where the value of your work lives in the output, the machine is coming for it; where it lives in the humans and context around the output, it isn’t. A verifiable output is a cost function with extra steps, and optimizing against a fixed target is the one thing these systems are built to do. Does the code run, does the theorem hold, does the invoice reconcile — anything with an external standard to check against is, sooner or later, checkable by a machine. What has no external standard, only a person on the other end deciding how they feel, gives the optimizer nothing to grip.
Two familiar spectra are the same axis drawn on two maps. Across a company it runs Sales → Product → Tech: on the right the work is judged by whether the thing works — the part the machines take first; on the left by a person deciding whether to trust you, and trust has no unit test. Across a discipline it runs Art → Science: science is legible by construction — verifiable claims, reproducible methods, the native habitat of an optimizer — while art is a blend of components that each carry science and meaning but whose mixture dissolves into something that communicates beneath the logical layer, where feeling is the only referee. Same line both times. So the advice falls out clean: lean left. With one honest caveat — the machines don’t stop at a line, they advance, and the frontier moves left over time. Leaning left doesn’t buy a fortress. It buys the longest runway.
It’s tempting to say the machines will just make better art, the way engines make better chess, and it won’t matter because the audience isn’t buying optimality. That’s wrong twice. Chess has a scoreboard: checkmate is checkmate, the target sits still, an engine climbs past every human and stays there. Art has no scoreboard — there’s no technically superior painting, because there’s no external standard the painting is trying to satisfy. Duchamp settled this in 1917 by submitting a factory-made urinal, signing it with a fake name, and titling it Fountain; it became one of the most consequential objects of twentieth-century art, its craft zero and its novelty of form zero. Its entire value is context, story, and the gesture of a human choosing to call it art. And where chess’s target sits still, art’s runs away: the instant a machine masters a look, that look curdles into “AI slop” and the human eye recoils and relocates. You can’t summit a peak that turns to swamp the moment you plant the flag.
The usual “humans differentiate, machines chase” line is true but told too vaguely. The mechanism is attestation. In the old world a typo marked you as careless; in a world where flawless, frictionless text is the free default of every machine, the typo flips sign — it becomes costly proof that a human was here and meant it. Imperfection becomes signature. The machine can then learn to fake the wobble, so it’s a chase — but the chase is the oldest engine in culture, not something new to AI: a style starts at the top, the tiers below imitate it, and the instant the copy is complete the thing dies at the top and moves on, because everyone now has the old thing. It’s the whole physics of trends and of cool. AI just becomes the fastest imitator ever built and turns the crank faster. But faster isn’t infinitely fast: the floor speed is set not by how fast the machine can copy but by how fast humans can notice, tire, and re-differentiate — a cognitive clock that doesn’t scale with compute, the same way knowing more people stalled at 150 no matter how much network we built. Your differentiator is, by definition, whatever the crowd hasn’t reached yet. The gap doesn’t close. Differentiation is a positional good, and positional scarcity is conserved by construction.
The scarcity that can’t be printed
Hedonic adaptation alone doesn’t win this argument. “We always want more” has an obvious rebuttal: so make more, forever — which is exactly what abundance promises. The thing that defeats abundance is subtler. Abundance is a claim about production, about how much can be made. But satisfaction isn’t an event in the warehouse; it’s an event in a nervous system, and that system has fixed properties no volume of supply can touch. It habituates — whatever you give it becomes the new zero. It’s finite — one lifetime, one serial stream of attention, only so much taken in before you die. And it grades on a curve — it reads rank, rarity, provenance, stakes, never absolute quantity. Every scarcity that outlives AGI lives in there, on the consumption side, in the architecture of the consumer.
Social scarcity is the sharpest instance, because rank is defined as zero-sum — which is why this essay spent its length there. But it isn’t the only one, and here I’ll plant a flag for another day rather than pretend to resolve it. Attention is capped by cognition — a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention. Time is capped by mortality; infinite production of experiences buys no more life to spend on them. Meaning seems to need stakes, and stakes need the genuine possibility of loss that abundance is busy engineering away. Each is a scarcity production can’t reach; each could carry its own essay. This one only had to make the first case.
Which brings it back to UBI — where the thing I’ve been arguing against turns out not to be the actual idea. Trace universal basic income to the people who argued it seriously, and the utopia isn’t there. It was first proposed as justice — compensation for a common inheritance of land that private property had enclosed. It was revived as efficiency — cash as a cleaner way to relieve poverty than a sprawling welfare bureaucracy, tuned to keep the incentive to work intact. Its modern form is a displacement argument — the machines take the jobs, so people need a floor. Three proposals across three centuries, and not one promises freedom from wanting. They promise a floor. And the floor is real and it matters enormously: a person in pain from hunger or untreated illness is not running anyone’s status race, and AGI dragging billions out of poverty and disease would be among the largest goods a technology could ever do. Nothing here is an argument against it.
The promise of freedom lives in the phrase, not the policy. “Universal basic income” sounds like the end of the struggle, and where the phrase is vague the imagination fills in the rest: free income plus infinite production equals rest. That equation is the thing I’m against — and we’ve already watched it fail. Give people money with no strings, as several large trials now have, and the one thing that reliably does not happen is that they stop. Employment holds or rises, people start businesses, the mental-health numbers improve while the striving does not. Hand a human being the floor and they start climbing again immediately, because the climbing was never about the floor.
So the honest picture is one scale, not two. Plot satisfaction against material resources: a steep climb on the left, then a long flat shelf — /‾‾‾‾. Down in the steep part, resources are everything; a person there is cold, sick, afraid of next month, and money changes their life in a way that is neither positional nor imaginary. But infinite production doesn’t build a second, higher curve to climb onto. It slides everyone rightward along the same one, and the right end is flat. And the most miserable person in any room is almost never standing in the steep part — they’re out on the flat shelf, suffering anyway, not from a scarcity of matter but from where they sit relative to everyone else. There is no “real pain” track that money fixes and a separate “luxury pain” track it can’t. One axis, one substrate — and past the steep part, adding resources just flattens the slope you’re already on. It can’t lift you onto higher ground, because there is no higher ground.
Keynes saw all of this in 1930. He got the productivity exactly right, he knew the relative needs would never be filled, and he bet against them anyway. His warning sits in the same essay as his bet:

“Yet there is no country and no people, I think, who can look forward to the age of leisure and of abundance without a dread. For we have been trained too long to strive and not to enjoy.”

Take the dread seriously. Not because abundance isn’t coming — it is, for everything that can be produced. But the thing we actually want was never on that list.

References
Kept out of the body deliberately — the arguments should stand on their own reasoning, not on names most readers don’t know. Listed here so the attribution is honest.

Keynes, J. M. (1930). Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren. — the leisure prediction, absolute vs. relative needs, and the “dread” passage.
Brickman, P., Coates, D., & Janoff-Bulman, R. (1978). Lottery winners and accident victims: Is happiness relative? JPSP, 36(8). — the hedonic-treadmill study.
Nisbett, R. E., & Wilson, T. D. (1977). Telling more than we can know. Psychological Review, 84(3). — no introspective access to our own reasons.
Gazzaniga, M. — the split-brain “interpreter” that confabulates reasons.
Johansson, P., Hall, L., et al. — choice-blindness experiments (people defend choices they never made).
Girard, R. (1961). Deceit, Desire and the Novel. — mimetic desire (used here as the foil, not the frame).
Anderson, C., Hildreth, J. A. D., & Howland, L. (2015). Is the desire for status a fundamental human motive? Psychological Bulletin, 141(3). — status as a universal primary drive.
Veblen, T. (1899). The Theory of the Leisure Class. — “conspicuous consumption.”
Hirsch, F. (1976). Social Limits to Growth. — the material/positional distinction.
Frank, R. (1985/1999). Choosing the Right Pond / Luxury Fever. — positional arms races.
Dunbar, R. (1992/1993). Neocortex size as a constraint on group size. J. Human Evolution / BBS.
Brown, D. (1991). Human Universals. — status/prestige as documented universals.
Boehm, C. (1999). Hierarchy in the Forest. — the “reverse dominance hierarchy” in egalitarian foragers.
Clark & Oswald (1994); Winkelmann & Winkelmann (1998); Lucas, Clark, Georgellis & Diener (2004). — unemployment’s non-pecuniary cost and permanent scarring.
Eisenberger, Lieberman & Williams (2003); DeWall et al. (2010). — social-pain / physical-pain overlap and acetaminophen. Strict single-region claims contested by Wager et al. (2016).
Easterlin, R. (1974); Luttmer, E. (2005), “Neighbors as Negatives,” QJE, 120(3). — relative income and the reference group.
Bellaiche, L., et al. (2023). Humans versus AI. Cognitive Research, 8(42). — identical art rated higher when labeled human-made.
Duchamp, M. (1917). Fountain.
Simmel, G. (1904). Fashion. — the imitation/differentiation trend cycle.
Simon, H. (1971). — “a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention.”
UBI provenance: Paine, Agrarian Justice (1797); Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (1962); modern trials — Finland (2017–18), Stockton SEED (2019–21), GiveDirectly Kenya.

Philosophy/Logic-Isn't-About-Truth.title: Logic Isn't About Truth
Philosophy/Logic-Isn't-About-Truth.content:
What logic is, and what it costs to mistake it for a truth machine

Most people treat logic as a machine for finding the truth: feed in facts, turn the handle, and truth comes out the other end. I think that’s wrong, and the mistake is expensive. It’s behind cults, behind smug atheism, behind half the pointless arguments on the internet, and behind a lot of quiet guilt people carry about being “inconsistent”.
So this piece does two things. First, what logic actually is. Second, what it costs not to know.
Logic needs someone doing it
Reality doesn’t do logic. It just happens. A rock falls, and nobody concludes anything.
Logic shows up only when there’s an observer: something that holds a model of reality inside itself. Sometimes the model copies the structure of the thing directly, the way you can picture a room with your eyes closed. Sometimes it uses symbols that stand in for the thing: words, numbers, equations. Either way, it’s a mirror.
But an observer doesn’t just mirror how things are right now. It learns how they behave, what pushes what and what follows what. Then it runs that behaviour forward inside its model to predict what happens next.
That’s where logic lives, and every piece of it has two parts:

An assertion: a bet that reality will keep behaving the way it has. Everything I’ve dropped has fallen, so this will fall. It’s a claim about the future, made from observations of the past.
A representation: reality mirrored in language, so the bet can be stated, combined with other bets, and pushed further.

Maths: the model that outgrows its source
Mathematics is the cleanest example. Counting starts as a mirror: three sheep, three pebbles. Numbers are abstract, but they’re mapped to something real. Algebra, calculus and differential equations are built further along the same road, from observations of quantity, change and motion.
Then maths does something stranger. Once you have a model, you can extend it past anything that exists. No number multiplied by itself gives −1. Mathematicians in the 1500s assumed one anyway, later called it i, and kept every other rule the same. They did it to solve equations, not to describe shapes.
And the made-up thing mapped back onto reality, somewhere nobody expected. Multiplying by i turns out to be a quarter turn, so complex numbers became a language for rotation and geometry, then for alternating current, and eventually for quantum mechanics. The foundations weren’t taken from geometry at all, and yet the result describes geometry. The physicist Eugene Wigner called this “the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics”. To me it’s the most beautiful thing about the subject: build an honest model, follow its rules past the edge of what you’ve seen, and it sometimes finds things before you do.
Why you never reach absolute truth
Every model starts from observation, and observation is limited. The limit that matters most is time.
To know something is absolutely true, you’d have to watch it hold across all of time. You can’t; you only ever see a stretch of it. Bertrand Russell’s chicken is the classic picture. The farmer feeds it every morning, and every morning the chicken’s model of the world is confirmed again, right up to the morning he wrings its neck.
So every claim about the world, however well tested, is a hypothesis. David Hume saw this in the 1700s. Karl Popper later built a philosophy of science on it: one clear failure can disprove a theory, but no number of successes can finally prove it.
Logic is a motion, not a position
If logic can’t hand you absolute truth, what is it? I think of it as a motion rather than a position. Logic isn’t a piece of information. It’s how you move through information: how you extend it, and how you get new information out of what you already have.
The formal version is simple. You start with axioms, statements you assume rather than prove. You apply rules of inference: if A implies B, and B implies C, then A implies C. What grows out of that is a tree of consequences, and the whole thing is a framework.
The axioms have only a couple of requirements. They shouldn’t contradict each other, and ideally none of them should follow from the others. Nothing requires them to come from reality. We’ve already seen that: √−1 is nonsense as a fact about the world, and the framework built on it is one of the most useful things humans own.
Look across the sciences and it’s the same shape every time:

Physics: make observations, build a framework from them, use it to predict.
Mathematics: choose axioms (often observations in disguise), build a framework, and it predicts, sometimes in fields it was never meant for.
Biology, and the rest of science: observe, model, predict, revise.

Logicians have a precise way to say this. An argument is valid if the conclusion follows from the premises. It’s sound if it’s valid and the premises are true. “All cats can fly; Tom is a cat; so Tom can fly” is perfectly valid and completely unsound. Logic only guarantees validity. Truth has to come in from outside, through the premises, and logic can’t check them for you.
That leads somewhere surprising: it’s very hard to be illogical. However much nonsense someone talks, they’re still chaining one thing to another, A to B to C. Even a bare claim with nothing derived from it is a framework, just one with a single node. When we call someone illogical, we usually mean one of two things: they’re reasoning from axioms we don’t share, or one of their steps doesn’t follow.
The cost of not knowing
Truth stops being the point
Physics isn’t supposed to be true. It’s supposed to predict. Newton’s laws are, strictly speaking, wrong; Einstein replaced them. Engineers still use them every day, because within their range they predict superbly. The statistician George Box put it best: “All models are wrong, but some are useful.”
Being closer to the truth usually helps a framework do its job, and that’s exactly why people confuse the two. Truth correlates with good logic, but it isn’t what makes reasoning logical. And sometimes the two come far apart, especially in philosophy and in relationships, where the most accurate thing isn’t always the best thing. Telling someone their cooking is mediocre on the night they cook for you may be true. It’s not what the evening is for.
This was the first big unlock for me. Once philosophy didn’t have to be true, I could point it at what I actually want from it, which is peace, and optimise for that directly. It’s working out really well. It lets me hold beliefs like nothing is all that serious, which has a nihilistic edge, without defending them as facts about the universe. They only have to do their job. (You can make truth the goal of a philosophy. You just have to choose it explicitly.) I’ve worked this out at length in Microframeworks.
Cults and the clever atheist make the same mistake
People get pulled into cults by someone claiming to know the absolute truth. Sometimes that person is a liar, and sometimes they’re sincerely fooled by their own brain. Either way, they’re using a relative instrument to sell an absolute. If you understand what logic is, you’ll never try to prove God with it, in the sense of establishing a final fact.
The other side makes the same mistake in reverse, using science to “prove” that religion is nonsense. I was one of them as a teenager: I’m so scientific, so logical, and all this religion and spirituality is unscientific bullshit. I was the clown there. I’d taken logic for a truth machine and was waving it at people.
Judged by usefulness, by what it predicts or how much peace it brings, God can be perfectly logical. Belief may have brought order to societies when it arose. Human brains relate to idols, and idolising motivates. Some feelings may only be available to people who believe. Decode the psychology and you could probably justify much of the value belief brings. The cultist and the clever atheist end up where they are for the same reason: they think logic is about truth.
One case against a general claim
This one is so common it drives me up the wall, and it runs both ways.
A counterexample against a tendency. You say “smoking generally shortens your life”, and someone replies “my grandfather smoked forty a day and lived to ninety-five”. When did I say always? A counterexample destroys a universal claim: one black swan and nobody can say “all swans are white” again. It barely dents a statistical one. One grandfather doesn’t move the curve.
A single case turned into a rule. The reverse is just as common. One bad meal and the restaurant is terrible. One friend’s startup fails and startups are a scam. One instance shows that something can happen. It says almost nothing about how often.
Both mistakes come from the same gap: not seeing that “always”, “usually” and “once” are different kinds of claim, which need different kinds of evidence.
You’re allowed to be more than one framework
This last one looks like a different topic, but it grows from the same root, and it’s the reason I can enjoy dark humour.
People feel a strong pull to fit their whole life into one consistent framework, because hypocrisy feels repulsive. So they enforce it on others: you laughed at a joke about someone in hospital, so you’re insensitive. That only works if a person is one belief system, one constitution, one truth.
A person isn’t. A person is a mix of many frameworks, and our wiring couldn’t hold to just one even if we tried. You can laugh at dark humour and still be kind, just as someone who eats meat can still have deep empathy. You don’t owe anyone a reconciliation. Walt Whitman got there first: “Do I contradict myself? Very well then I contradict myself, (I am large, I contain multitudes.)”
A lot of cognitive dissonance, the discomfort of holding beliefs that seem to clash, comes from thinking that being logical means having one framework. It doesn’t. Your beliefs can depend on context. What makes them look contradictory is that the context has been stripped out. Put it back, and they often fit inside one larger framework that is perfectly consistent.

Logic is a way of moving, not a place to arrive. Once you know that, you stop asking it for what it can’t give you, which is certainty, and use it for what it’s good at: getting you, one step at a time, wherever you’ve decided to go.

Philosophy/Microframeworks.title: Microframeworks
Philosophy/Microframeworks.content:
On logic, the self, and the quiet engineering of peace


                  
                  Working draft 
                  
                

This is the current state of a book I’m writing. The ideas are still being argued over and tested, and the last section lists what’s unresolved. Treat it as a map in progress, not a finished doctrine.



This is a philosophy about how to live, and I want to build it the way a mathematician builds a theorem: from foundations you can inspect, one step at a time.
So it starts with logic, which is an unusual place to start a philosophy of life. Every claim that follows is a piece of reasoning, and you have a right to know what reasoning is before I do any of it on you. From there it moves the way I actually moved through these ideas. It examines what we are chasing, builds a model of the system we live inside, watches the most popular model of the self fail, and replaces it with something else: a picture of the mind as a changing field of small, temporary logical worlds. I call them microframeworks.
I won’t claim any of these models is true in a final, metaphysical sense. By the end of the first section you’ll see why I think “useful” is the better test. The question to ask of everything here is not “do you believe it?” but “does holding it leave you more at peace, across more of your life, than what you held before?”
Some of these ideas will sound like they belong to old traditions: Buddhism, Advaita Vedanta, the Stoics, karma yoga. They do. I didn’t start there and decorate the argument with quotations. I started with logic and observation and kept arriving, slightly startled, at doorways those traditions carved centuries ago. I’ve left those arrivals in, because it means something when independent roads meet. But the road is the point.
Who this is for
This is for someone who already wants something: less stress, more peace, or a way to understand why their own motivations keep contradicting each other.
Start with the purpose you already have. Your work, your family, your country, a personal ambition. I’m not going to tell you it’s worthless. I’m going to ask you to look at the relationship between that purpose, your sense of who you are, and your peace. The question at the centre of all of this is simple:

If you’ll be at peace once you’ve done this thing, why can’t you be at peace first, and then do it?

There is a cost. To get anything from this philosophy you have to be willing to create some distance from your purposes: to see where they came from, how far they reach, and how much authority they really have. Distance doesn’t mean abandoning them. It means you stop treating them as the condition for being allowed to be at peace. Not everyone will want to pay that cost, and this isn’t written to persuade everyone.
1. Logic: the instrument
Logic, as I use the word, is a way of navigating information. You start from assumptions — axioms — and you draw implications from them with rules of inference. If A implies B and B implies C, then A implies C. A set of axioms plus the rules for building on them is a framework.
Mathematics shows how far this goes. Take the square root of minus one. It sounds like nonsense: no number squares to a negative. Assume it anyway, and you get complex numbers, which are beautiful, consistent and indispensable to physics. Negate Euclid’s parallel postulate and you get geometries that turned out to describe curved spacetime. Starting assumptions that look absurd can support perfectly valid frameworks.
So what varies between frameworks is not whether they are logical but whether they are useful. In physics, usefulness means matching observation. In a philosophy of life, I’ll measure it by how much peace a framework brings.
This leads to my first strong claim: all human reasoning happens inside some framework, including reasoning we call superstitious, emotional or irrational. “That’s illogical” usually means “that doesn’t follow from the assumptions I’m using.” The belief may follow perfectly well from someone else’s. Emotions aren’t outside logic either. They run on different axioms: biological drives, past experience, survival instincts.
That doesn’t mean mistakes are impossible. Take the classic error. “If it rains, the pavement gets wet” and “the pavement is wet” do not together imply that it rained; the pavement could be wet for other reasons. Someone who concludes it rained has made an invalid inference. But they can then adopt “wet pavement means rain” as a new assumption, and from that amended framework the rain conclusion follows validly, even though the new assumption is false about the world. People do this constantly. A conclusion reached badly becomes a premise for everything after it.
So three questions need to stay separate:

Does this conclusion follow from these premises?
Are the premises true, or useful, in this context?
Are these really the premises this person was using?

Most arguments about whether someone is “being logical” mix all three. And this philosophy has to pass the same examination it applies to everything else. Its assumptions are open to inspection too.
2. Peace, not happiness
What are we actually chasing? The obvious answer is happiness. I think that answer comes from mistaking a correlation for the thing itself.
If happiness were the point, we wouldn’t watch sad films. We wouldn’t scream at a football match with our hearts pounding in something close to rage, or eat food so spicy it hurts, or ride roller coasters, or go to horror films, or love the strain of an arm-wrestle. In each case the experience is unpleasant by any emotional measure, and yet we don’t want it to stop. That last part is the test. It isn’t pain followed by a reward, like an ice bath you endure for the glow afterwards. It’s pain while not wanting the experience to be otherwise.
That is what I mean by peace:

Desire is a tendency to move towards some outcome — wanting things to change.
Peace is when the framework you’re currently in isn’t struggling to reject or escape what it’s experiencing.

Peace can come with any emotional tone. Sadness can be peaceful. Anger at a match can be peaceful. Happiness can come without peace, as in the anxious high of something you’re afraid to lose. Peace isn’t a particular feeling. It’s a relationship to whatever you’re feeling.
I once believed something stronger: that peace is secretly what everyone is pursuing, whatever they say their goal is. When any plan completes, you stop wanting change with respect to it, so peace looks like the shape every plan ends in. I still find that intuition compelling, but I no longer need it. The weaker claim is enough. Many people, looking honestly at their lives, find that the cycle of wanting, getting, briefly settling and wanting again isn’t satisfying. For them, peace is a coherent thing to aim at directly. That’s the invitation.
3. Why understand the system at all
Imagine living in a house you don’t understand, or using a laptop where you only know three settings. When nothing goes wrong, you get by fine. When something does, you’re helpless, because the failure means nothing to you.
The body and mind are like that. If you don’t understand how impulses, emotions, attention and habits work, your peace depends on luck: on nothing going wrong. Understanding the mechanics doesn’t make you immune to bad luck, but it gives you better ways to predict and respond.
And you don’t have infinite lives to find out by trial and error what works. You can’t run a statistical study on your own existence. So I want to understand the system the way physics understands the universe, by building a model from observations, not by collecting tips.
Physics can’t cut the universe open either. It builds abstractions, tests them against what it sees, and keeps the ones that predict well. We can do the same with the mind. A model doesn’t have to be a complete account of the brain to be useful. It has to explain what we observe well enough to act on.
4. The first observation: evolution
Start with the oldest and most powerful explanation of why living things behave as they do. DNA that copies itself more effectively becomes more common. Run that rule for a few billion years and you get everything.
Nearly everything we feel traces back to it. Poison tastes bitter. Rot smells foul. Children fear the dark, because the dark is where predators hunted. Sugar tastes wonderful and vegetables don’t, because our ancestors needed dense calories fast.
The lesson is that our preferences, instincts and emotional reactions aren’t personal truths handed down from somewhere. They’re the logic of survival running through us. Evolution installed a large set of default frameworks, triggered by the world around us. Some axioms come pre-installed: I am important. I must look after myself. I must be respected. They’re reinforced by emotion, and they will resist any philosophy that questions them. Keep an eye out for that resistance as you read.
5. The familiar model: a self at war with its mind
Ask anyone who they are and they’ll point to their body. Ask them how they control it and you get a familiar picture: there’s me, the conscious, intelligent self, and there’s my mind, a powerful but dumb machine of habits, memories and impulses. I set the goals. The mind is supposed to carry them out, but it has its own agenda and enormous inertia.
Picture two people sharing one laptop and fighting over the keyboard. The self has awareness but limited bandwidth, and can only attend to a few things at once. The mind does most of the actual work through reflex, learning and memory. Train it badly and it’s hard to retrain. Go against its conditioning and it punishes you with emotion.
This model underlies an enormous amount of human wisdom. Buddhist mindfulness observes the mind and stops following its impulses. Karma yoga has the self act while the mind learns. Stoicism, and nearly every self-help book, is about the self mastering the mind. It’s a useful model, and it worked for me for a long time.
Then it started producing two problems.
Action paralysis. If you take seriously that worldly goals are ultimately empty, motivation for ordinary practical goals drains away. But the impulses you’ve devalued don’t stop. They keep running your behaviour, just without your endorsement.
Endless frustration. Why can’t I just take control? Why do I need tricks and crutches? Why can’t I be fully disciplined starting today? Worse, the model poisons good experiences after the fact. You work passionately for hours, and afterwards a voice says that wasn’t really you, that was ambition, you weren’t self-aware. Every experience becomes an interrogation of motives.
The war never ends. Even an enlightened person screams under torture, so enlightenment isn’t a switch you flip. It’s a spectrum, and the fight has a ceiling. A framework meant to bring peace had become a reliable source of frustration. That’s what sent me back to observation.
6. Dissolving the self
Look closely at a sentence like “I didn’t want to do it, but my mind made me.” Afterwards we say “that wasn’t me.” Who is the “I” in each half of that sentence?
When I solve a maths problem, it feels like I am doing it. When an impulse takes over, it feels like my mind did it. But the line between them won’t hold still. Physically, there is no separate self and no separate mind. There is one system, a body and brain interacting with an environment, and “self” and “mind” are abstractions we draw over its behaviour.
Two well-known lines of research make this vivid. In split-brain patients, the hemispheres are surgically disconnected. Show an instruction only to the non-verbal half, and the patient acts on it. Ask the verbal half why, and it doesn’t say “I don’t know.” It invents a confident, plausible reason on the spot. And in blindsight, people with damage to the visual cortex who report seeing nothing can still point to objects far better than chance. A great deal of processing happens beneath the layer that narrates.
I offer these as illustrations, not proof of everything that follows. But they point to what the war model got wrong. The wanting, the resisting, the doing and the regretting are all the same system. Guilt and frustration come from forcing a two-entity story onto it.
7. Microframeworks
If there’s no single self, what is the “I” that wants things?
Look at how “I” behaves across a day. Sometimes I want to work hard. Sometimes I want balance and rest. Sometimes I want company, sometimes solitude. Each of these comes with its own priorities, its own sense of what matters, its own idea of who I am. These aren’t moods of one fixed self. Each is a different “I”, defined inside a different framework.
A microframework is a temporary configuration of assumptions, available information, priorities and self-reference. What distinguishes one from another is mostly its axioms: what it takes for granted. Each supplies its own meaning for the word “I”. It might mean the body, a role, an ambition or an observer.
Two images help.
Peripheral vision. Your eyes can only focus on a small area; the rest is blur. Inside a framework, it’s the same. You reason sharply about a few things, while most of your assumptions sit blurry at the edges: inherited, trusted, triggered, never examined.
The spotlight. Picture all possible reasoning as a vast tree, and a spotlight that lights up only a small part of it at a time. The lit region is the active framework. You don’t choose where the spotlight goes. It flickers, moved by your surroundings, your memories, your body’s state and your conditioning. A framework doesn’t have to finish its goal before the spotlight moves on. Its concern can go dark and come back later.
Nobody stands outside the system choosing which framework runs. The choosing itself happens inside some framework.
This changes how to plan. If your present intention isn’t a permanent controller, plan for your future changes of mind. Deleting Instagram from your phone isn’t an admission that you’re weak. It’s sensible preparation by a framework that knows a different framework will be in charge at eleven tonight.
8. Desire, regret and self-control
With this model, desire becomes simpler. A desire is the system’s tendency to move towards some outcome. The framework that’s currently evaluating may endorse that tendency or oppose it. The outcome may be available or out of reach.

Endorsed and out of reach, desire feels like longing or frustration.
Endorsed and available, it feels like anticipation or excitement.
Opposed and out of reach, it’s an uncomfortable awareness of wanting something you don’t want to want.
Opposed and available, it’s open conflict, like the smoker with a cigarette in front of them.

“Desire overpowered my will” is one interpretation of that last case. It isn’t what desire is.
Regret looks different too. The framework judging yesterday’s action has different priorities from the framework that acted. “I had no self-control” is a statement made from inside one framework about another, with no special authority over it. You didn’t fail at self-control. You were a different “I”.
This isn’t a licence for anything. Frameworks affect one another through the body they share. One framework finds peace in junk food, and that conditions the system so later frameworks are more sluggish and anxious. That is what I mean by karma: not moral bookkeeping, just mechanical consequence between frameworks. Garbage in, garbage out. Discipline still matters, but it works by shaping conditions, not by an inner commander winning a fight.
9. Purpose and its scope
Where do our purposes come from? Personal history, upbringing, culture, and the survival logic evolution installed. Seeing that doesn’t make a purpose false. You can understand exactly why you care about your family and care about them just as much. But it does change how much automatic authority a purpose gets. Trust inherited purposes a little less automatically. Treat them as revisable.
Here is where I’m a nihilist, and I want to be precise about it. All mattering happens inside frameworks. Brushing your teeth matters a great deal to the framework doing it, and less to a framework planning your whole day. Your country matters intensely within patriotic frameworks. None of this is fake. What I deny is that any purpose has authority outside every framework, written into the universe and binding regardless of perspective. Things matter locally. Nothing is commanded absolutely.
That’s what creating distance means. You don’t stop caring. You see the scope of each care: where it came from, which frameworks it belongs to, and that being at peace doesn’t have to wait for it.
10. Creating distance
I came to this through a question about what we’re really after when we want things. I used to picture desired objects as ways of buying an emotional currency from the body: the car buys pride, the holiday buys joy. Could you get the currency without paying for the object? Then I noticed the currency wasn’t happiness. Sometimes happiness felt wrong and sadness felt right. What I valued was a way of relating to experience, not one kind of experience.
Then there’s the treadmill. You want something, you work for it, you get it, you feel settled for a while, and then the wanting starts again on something new. Many people notice this and conclude they just haven’t found the right thing yet. Another conclusion is available: the problem isn’t the object, it’s the condition you attached to peace.
So distance can be taken at different depths:

Keep your purpose fully, but explore whether less attachment to its outcome makes you steadier and more effective.
Examine where it came from, question how necessary it really is, and loosen how much of your identity rests on it.
Choose peace itself as your broader orientation, and keep pursuing other purposes as commitments you endorse.

Think of a patriot who keeps serving their country while seeing their patriotism as conditioned, local and lacking absolute authority. They still serve. They’re just no longer at war with every setback.
11. The orchestrator
Something in you is reading this and thinking about how to live better. Call it the orchestrator: the family of frameworks that understands this model, reflects on purposes and tries to coordinate the rest.
It isn’t a controller outside the system, sneaking the old self back in. It runs on the same substrate as everything else and has influence only when the conditions for it arise. Tonight, the spotlight will move and the orchestrator will go dark. That’s expected.
Here is the key difference from the war model. The war model believed its “I”. The orchestrator employs its “I”. The war model took the single self as fact. There really was a war and a self who should win, so every loss was a real failure, and guilt was built in. The orchestrator uses “I” as a working assumption, the way a mathematician uses the square root of minus one, fully aware that identities map to frameworks. When another framework takes over, “that was a different I” is already part of its understanding. Nothing to feel guilty about. The fix wasn’t abolishing “I”. It was demoting it from truth to axiom.
Inside the orchestrator’s outlook, peace requires nothing: no achievement, no justification, no change. That doesn’t mean the orchestrator is always active. Whether it appears, stays and gets recalled depends on the substrate. Those two facts don’t conflict.
And the orchestrator isn’t the only place peace lives. Ordinary frameworks find peace whenever their own conditions are met: you finish the project, you eat the meal, the argument resolves. The aim isn’t to spend as much time as possible in the orchestrator. It’s to make peace more common across all the frameworks of a life.
That gives the orchestrator a job: coordination. A good company doesn’t need every employee to share one personality or motive. It needs ambition, curiosity, care and enjoyment pulling in roughly compatible directions instead of sabotaging each other. The orchestrator works the same way. It uses ordinary judgment to resolve conflicts. It doesn’t need a perfect algorithm. And it works mostly through conditioning: what you learn, what you remember, how you arrange your surroundings, which triggers you remove and which useful responses you make easy to reach.
This also answers the obvious objection: the orchestrator wants other frameworks to be at peace, and wanting is desire, so isn’t it just another desiring framework? Yes. Something is always running. Being frameworkless isn’t on the menu; the only question is which framework runs. Given that, the orchestrator is the best available occupant of the slot, because its running conditions the system towards more peace overall. And its wanting has a particular character: full engagement, with nothing missing. Not wanting from lack, but wanting as play.
12. Living it: karma yoga and Lila
In practice this is a pitch to become a karmayogi: keep working towards your goals with full commitment, with greater distance from their outcomes and more ability to handle what you feel along the way. It’s close to what some people call optimistic nihilism. Nothing is commanded absolutely, so you’re free to play your roles fully.
Lila, the Hindu idea of divine play, captures the spirit. Krishna knows the cosmic drama is a drama and plays each role with complete passion anyway. You can inhabit your roles — engineer, parent, friend, citizen — without needing one rigid identity underneath them, and without needing any of them to be the final truth about you.
Some practical consequences:

Let every motive contribute. Ambition, curiosity, affection and enjoyment are all fuel. The goal isn’t to suppress emotion, it’s to coordinate it.
Prepare for the spotlight to move. Change your environment, remove predictable triggers, make good responses easy. That’s engineering, not weakness.
Use frustration as a cue. When you catch yourself condemning a past action, that’s a signal to understand the conditions that produced it and work on those.
Expect to forget. You’ll get absorbed, lose the outlook and get lost in pursuit again. That doesn’t invalidate it. The outlook shifts gradually, across many frameworks, not once and for all.

It also explains the ceiling on enlightenment. Conditioning reshapes where the spotlight tends to land. It never pins the spotlight down, because nobody is holding it. Under extreme enough stimulus, such as torture, it gets dragged regardless. That isn’t a self losing a fight. A distribution can be shifted but not frozen. That’s also why enlightenment is a spectrum, not a switch.
And it explains what reading something like this does. It isn’t instructions to a controller, because there’s no controller to instruct. It’s conditioning. It reshapes the landscape so that frameworks like the orchestrator light up a little more often.
13. Further: ego and the universal observer
This last part is a branch I hold for practical reasons, and I want to be clear about that.
In this account, ego is the bias that gives one body and its identity special importance. Evolution installed it, and it’s very useful for survival. But why should the boundary of the body also be the boundary of what I care about, or of what I identify with?
Consider seeing red. Everything your body does in response to red — naming it, reacting to it — is information processing. Now imagine your experience of red and blue were swapped, but all the processing stayed the same. Your behaviour would be identical, yet something would differ: the felt quality of the experience. That suggests experience isn’t exhausted by what the body does. It opens a slot for something beyond function: an observer.
How many observers? This is a fork, and I don’t think it can be settled by derivation. So I settle it the way the logic section said to, by usefulness.

One observer per body reattaches ego at the deepest level: this awareness is mine. Optimising peace then collapses to optimising my own peace, and the cheapest route is withdrawal. Renounce everything and sit still. The rational endpoint is paralysis.
A single observer has no body boundary. “My peace” stops being a coherent goal and the scope becomes every framework, everywhere. Engaging with the world stays motivated, because that’s where other frameworks’ peace is decided.

The image I use is an auditorium with a single member of the audience and many performers, each in a separate room with its own window. Each performer knows only their own scene and can only talk about their own performance. The audience sees every room at once.
I don’t claim this is literally, metaphysically true. I keep it because a purely deflationary picture — I’m just neurons — tends to drain the reflective frameworks of their force, while this one keeps life vivid and keeps concern from collapsing back onto a single body. Whether it works that way for you is something to test, not accept.
Extending concern to peace across all frameworks, in every body, is my own ethical choice. The rest of this philosophy doesn’t require you to make it.
What remains open
This is a work in progress, and some things aren’t settled:

What counts as one framework? I need a way to identify frameworks that doesn’t just reconstruct their assumptions after the fact to explain anything at all.
Does distance keep motivation intact? My hypothesis is that creating distance preserves, or even improves, the ability to act and to handle emotion. That’s a practical claim, and it needs testing, not assertion.
How should incompatible interests be coordinated? Especially as the scope of concern widens.
The science. The claims about free will, consciousness, after-the-fact explanation and brain organisation need careful review. The experiments illustrate the model; they don’t prove the whole thing.
The observer. Its practical effects should be judged separately from whether it’s metaphysically real.

The one thing I’m confident of is the method: state your assumptions, reason carefully from them, and judge the result by whether it leaves you more at peace, across more of your life, than what you held before. Walk the road with me. Check each step. Refuse the ones that don’t hold.

index.content:
I’m Chinmay. This is where I write in public: longer pieces I’m working on, published as they evolve. Some of them are drafts, and they’ll change.
Philosophy
Microframeworks: my working philosophy of how to live. It starts from logic, takes apart the idea of a single self in charge of the mind, and replaces it with a changing field of small, temporary frameworks. It asks one question: can you be at peace first, and then do the thing?
Logic Isn’t About Truth: what logic is (a way of moving through information, not a machine that produces truth) and what it costs to mistake it for one.
Essays
The Scarcity That Survives: what AGI and universal basic income can and can’t change. Abundance solves production, not wanting, and the status race is the one scarcity no machine can flood.
The Cost of Needing to Understand Everything: for people who can’t learn anything until they understand it to the core, and blame their memory. How that bottom-up habit works, what it costs, and the shift to trusting abstractions.
